description: Machine credentials and secrets that commonly leak into server/application logs: JWTs, AWS access keys, PEM private-key blocks, vendor API tokens with documented fixed prefixes (GitHub, GitLab, Google, Slack, Stripe, Twilio, SendGrid, npm, Anthropic), HTTP Authorization credentials, connection-string and command-line passwords, installer properties, environment or config assignments, and the credentials a PowerShell script body writes in the language (credential objects, encoded commands, quoted keys, sigiled variables). These tokens are high-entropy and prefix/context-anchored, so the detectors are precise. Replacements are structurally valid for their kind but provably INVALID (they embed the literal REDACTED sentinel, which every detector's `safe` recognises) so a leaked credential is scrubbed before upload, not merely flagged.
notes: All replacements carry the literal 'REDACTED' sentinel (base64url-safe, so even a fake JWT or AKIA key stays shape-valid). Every detector therefore uses safe='REDACTED' for idempotency — the rare real secret that itself contains the substring 'redacted' is simply left alone, which is acceptable.

Vendor-token detectors anchor on the published PREFIX and require a body of at least the smallest width that vendor has minted; they do not pin an exact width and do not require a word boundary after the body. An exact width misses every other size the vendor mints, and a base64url body ending in a character with no boundary after it drops the token entirely, so both are leaks rather than precision. Their fakes KEEP the prefix so the log still reads like 'a <vendor> token was here'. Publishable/identifier variants are excluded on purpose: Stripe pk_, Twilio AC… account SID. SparkLogs' own prefixes (sl_, slk_, slr_) are covered here too: they are the credentials whose minting rules we control.
Bearer credentials that are JWTs are shaped back into a fake JWT; opaque tokens and Basic credentials become an opaque REDACTED token. AWS access keys keep the AKIA/ASIA + 20-char shape.

Every command-line pattern OPENS with the zero-width test that the value does not start with whitespace, ahead of its anchor look-behind, and the order is deliberate rather than stylistic. The look-behind is unbounded, so evaluating it costs work proportional to the line; the zero-width test costs nothing and rejects every start position inside a run of spaces before the look-behind is ever tried there. Moving it after the anchor makes no difference to what matches and made a pathological single-line input eight times slower.

Command-line detectors anchor on a TOOL NAME or on a proper-noun grammar, never on a flag letter alone. A single letter names something different on every tool, and anchoring on one was measured firing on hundreds of innocent command lines. The gap between a tool name and its flag stops at a command separator, so a match cannot reach into the next command on the line.

Entropy-only secrets with NO stable prefix (e.g. an AWS secret access key, generic 32-hex API keys) are deliberately NOT pattern-matched here: they would over-match in logs, and a downstream review layer covers those.

NO DETECTOR HERE ANCHORS ON A BARE WORD ANYWHERE IT APPEARS. Every one requires a key that ends in a credential word immediately before its separator, a quoted field name, a sigil in front of a flag or a variable name, a tool name, an argument position, a vendor prefix, or the START OF A LINE. A word alone is not a signal: `token`, `secret` and `bearer` are ordinary English, they appear in sentences that are not assignments, and a detector anchored on one wherever it stood was measured redacting `publicKeyToken=`, the phrase 'The token=X was rejected by the API', and, through a whitespace-tolerant separator, the first token of the FOLLOWING line.

The lowercase unsigiled spellings `api_key=`, `token:` and `secret=` are matched only where the key BEGINS a line, which is the environment and config file shape; the same words mid-sentence are not. Their uppercase environment-variable spellings are also covered by the installer-property rule, and their sigil-prefixed, JSON and connection-string forms by their own detectors. Widening the bare list to match those words anywhere is what dragged them into prose.

conn-string-password is space-tolerant and semicolon-tolerant only inside connection-string context (a neighbouring ';key=' on the line). A bare 'password=' in free prose or on a command line keeps the whitespace-terminated form, so an ordinary log sentence loses the credential and nothing else. Over-redaction of the surroundings is a product failure of its own: the user, host, database and command shape are the diagnostic value that survives redaction.

Quoted value branches require a delimiter after the closing quote. A quoted run that cannot close can always shorten itself to a shorter valid run, and a value opening with a doubled quote is exactly that shape, so the alternative to the requirement is a placeholder followed by the rest of the credential. Sending that text to an eat-to-end branch over-redacts the remainder of the line and leaks nothing, which is the trade this profile makes every time the two conflict.

Length ceilings on a CONTEXT run (a neighbouring key name, a URL userinfo username) are leaks, not limits: past the ceiling the match fails and the credential ships, or the value stops being bounded and eats the neighbour. Ceilings on the VALUE are a different matter and are not used either, since a credential has no maximum length worth guessing.

detectors.name: private-key-block
detectors.description: PEM-encoded private key block (RSA/EC/DSA/OpenSSH/PGP/encrypted). The whole block, including the armor lines, is replaced.

detectors.name: jwt
detectors.description: JSON Web Token. The 'eyJ' prefix is base64url of '{"' — a reliable JWT header signal — followed by header.payload(.signature).

detectors.name: aws-access-key
detectors.description: AWS access key id (AKIA long-term / ASIA temporary): a vendor-defined prefix + 16 uppercase-alnum chars, so essentially no false positives.

detectors.name: github-token
detectors.description: GitHub access token: a documented gh{p,o,u,s,r}_ prefix (personal/oauth/user-to-server/server-to-server/refresh) followed by a base62 body. The body length is a FLOOR, not an exact width, and there is no boundary requirement after it. A vendor mints tokens at whatever width it likes and has changed those widths before, so an exact width misses every other minted size, and a base64url body that happens to end in `-` or `_` has no word boundary after it at all, which drops the token entirely. Both failures ship the credential.

detectors.name: github-pat-fine
detectors.description: GitHub fine-grained personal access token: the github_pat_ prefix followed by a base62-and-underscore body. The body length is a FLOOR, not an exact width, and there is no boundary requirement after it. A vendor mints tokens at whatever width it likes and has changed those widths before, so an exact width misses every other minted size, and a base64url body that happens to end in `-` or `_` has no word boundary after it at all, which drops the token entirely. Both failures ship the credential.

detectors.name: gitlab-pat
detectors.description: GitLab personal access token: the glpat- prefix followed by a base64url body. The body length is a FLOOR, not an exact width, and there is no boundary requirement after it. A vendor mints tokens at whatever width it likes and has changed those widths before, so an exact width misses every other minted size, and a base64url body that happens to end in `-` or `_` has no word boundary after it at all, which drops the token entirely. Both failures ship the credential.

detectors.name: google-api-key
detectors.description: Google API key: the fixed AIza prefix followed by a base64url body. The body length is a FLOOR, not an exact width, and there is no boundary requirement after it. A vendor mints tokens at whatever width it likes and has changed those widths before, so an exact width misses every other minted size, and a base64url body that happens to end in `-` or `_` has no word boundary after it at all, which drops the token entirely. Both failures ship the credential.

detectors.name: slack-token
detectors.description: Slack token (xoxb/xoxp/xoxa/xoxr/xoxs/xoxe- bot/user/app/refresh/config/app-configuration prefix). The body length is a FLOOR, not an exact width, and there is no boundary requirement after it. A vendor mints tokens at whatever width it likes and has changed those widths before, so an exact width misses every other minted size, and a base64url body that happens to end in `-` or `_` has no word boundary after it at all, which drops the token entirely. Both failures ship the credential.

detectors.name: slack-webhook
detectors.description: Slack incoming-webhook URL; the team/channel/token path segments are the secret (the host is kept).

detectors.name: stripe-secret-key
detectors.description: Stripe secret/restricted key (sk_/rk_ live or test). Publishable pk_ keys are intentionally NOT matched (not secret).

detectors.name: twilio-api-key
detectors.description: Twilio API key SID (SK + 32 hex). The AC… account SID is an identifier, not a secret, and is not matched.

detectors.name: sendgrid-key
detectors.description: SendGrid API key (SG. + 22 chars + '.' + 43 chars).

detectors.name: npm-token
detectors.description: npm access token: the npm_ prefix followed by a base62 body. The body length is a FLOOR, not an exact width, and there is no boundary requirement after it. A vendor mints tokens at whatever width it likes and has changed those widths before, so an exact width misses every other minted size, and a base64url body that happens to end in `-` or `_` has no word boundary after it at all, which drops the token entirely. Both failures ship the credential.

detectors.name: sparklogs-ingest-key
detectors.description: SparkLogs ingest key: the sl_ prefix, a lowercase region label, and a base62 body. Our own credential, which is the one whose minting rules we control and therefore the one there is no excuse for missing.

detectors.name: sparklogs-agent-key
detectors.description: SparkLogs managed-agent key: the slk_ prefix followed by a lowercase hex body.

detectors.name: sparklogs-refresh-token
detectors.description: SparkLogs refresh token: the slr_ prefix and two base64url segments separated by a dot.

detectors.name: anthropic-key
detectors.description: Anthropic API key (sk-ant- prefix).

detectors.name: http-auth-credential
detectors.description: Credential in an HTTP `Authorization` or `Proxy-Authorization` header, in any of the schemes that carry one (Bearer, Basic, Digest, Negotiate, NTLM, ApiKey), as a header line, a curl argument or a JSON header object. THE HEADER NAME IS PART OF THE ANCHOR, and that is the difference between this and matching a scheme word alone. `Bearer`, `Basic` and `Negotiate` are ordinary English words that appear in prose, in release notes and in the phrase `the Authorization header was missing`, and a detector anchored on the word alone was measured firing on all of them. The scheme word survives, so a reader still sees which scheme was in use. The quoted branches require a delimiter after the closing quote: a doubled quote at the START of the value is a shorter valid quoted run, so without the requirement the empty pair matches and the credential behind it ships. The one-token branch stops at a comma or semicolon as well as at whitespace, because a header value list continues after those.

detectors.name: conn-string-url-password
detectors.description: Password embedded in a URL's userinfo, e.g. postgres://user:PASS@host. Only the password (between ':' and '@') is redacted; a host:port with no '@' is left alone. THE USERNAME RUN IS UNBOUNDED. A ceiling on it is a leak rather than a limit: a userinfo username longer than the ceiling fails the whole match, and the password after it then ships verbatim. Nothing about a long username makes the credential behind it less of a credential, and a token, an account id or a URL-encoded principal all routinely run past any figure that looks generous.

detectors.name: conn-string-password
detectors.description: Credential value in a `key=value` assignment: `Password=`, `pwd=`, `passwd=`, Azure `AccountKey=`, `AccessKey=`, `ClientSecret=`, `SharedAccessSignature=`, and the hyphen and underscore spellings of each. Only the value is replaced: the key, the separator and every neighbouring option survive, because the user, host, database and command shape are the diagnostic value that has to outlive redaction. AN OPTIONAL IDENTIFIER PREFIX in front of the key catches `SecretAccessKey=` and `AwsSecretAccessKey=`, which a bare word boundary misses because no boundary exists between a lowercase letter and an uppercase one; that form is the SECRET half of an AWS key pair. The key must still sit immediately before the `=`, so `MyPasswordPolicy=`, `PasswordExpiryDays=`, `LastPasswordChange=` and `accesskeyid=` (the PUBLIC half of the pair) are not matched. FIVE VALUE FORMS, tried in order. A QUOTED value, in either quote, ends at its closing quote and understands a doubled quote as an escaped one. That closing quote must be followed by a delimiter or the end of the line, and the requirement is what stops a partial redaction: a quoted run that cannot close can always SHORTEN itself to a shorter valid run, and a value opening with a doubled quote is exactly that shape, so without the requirement the empty pair matches, the placeholder lands, and the credential behind it ships. A value in CONNECTION-STRING CONTEXT (the key is preceded by `;key=`, or another `;key=` follows on the line) runs to a `;` that is followed by a plausible next key, or to the end of the line, so spaces and embedded semicolons inside the value are covered. Then the two UNTERMINATED-QUOTE fallbacks, which eat to the end of the line rather than leave half a credential behind. Last, a BARE value ends at whitespace: it consumes interior quotes, since an apostrophe is an ordinary character to a command interpreter and `password=don't` must go whole, but it backs off a trailing quote so the surrounding quoting stays balanced. THE KEY RUN IS UNBOUNDED AND UNICODE-AWARE, and both halves are load-bearing. A ceiling on the length of the following key name means a longer neighbour key is not recognised as a key at all, the value eats to the end of the line, and the neighbour the detector exists to preserve dies with it. `\w` is ASCII-only in JavaScript, so a key spelt in any other script would fail the same way; the Unicode property classes and the `u` flag are what keep an ordinary non-English log from over-redacting. THE VALUE MAY NOT BEGIN WITH WHITESPACE, which is a cost rule rather than a matching one: the separator run in front of it is variable-length, so without the rule a long run of spaces after an `=` would offer the engine one start position per space and each of them would re-scan the line. Every value form starts on a non-space character anyway, so nothing is lost. THE FLAG-TOKEN GUARD keeps the connection-string branch off a command line: `;word=` can appear anywhere, including inside a quoted argument, so without the guard `--account-key=K; --metadata "env=prod;tier=1"` would run the value across the rest of the command. A run that reaches whitespace followed by a flag sigil stops there.

detectors.name: powershell-variable-credential
detectors.description: Credential assigned to a PowerShell VARIABLE whose name ends in a credential word (`$apiKey = ...`, `$api_key = ...`, `$clientSecret = ...`). A script block reaches a log whole, so the assignment that feeds a later cmdlet is written in the language and no flag-anchored rule sees it. THE `$` SIGIL IS THE ANCHOR and it is what makes this key list safe: `api_key` is the spelling a sentence uses (`Starting worker with api_key=abc123 and region=us-east-1`), and the same words with no sigil in front of them are left to the key=value rule, whose narrower list keeps them out of prose. A variable name is not prose. The name must END with the credential word immediately before the `=`, so `$apiKeyPath` and `$passwordPolicy` keep their values, and an unquoted value stops at a `;` so the next statement on the line survives. PROVENANCE: OBSERVED collector literal `_prose_kv` in the SparkLogs source library (`stdlib/6_pack_finalize.vrl`) at 7bb901b, narrowed to the sigiled spelling.

detectors.name: json-credential-value
detectors.description: Credential value in a JSON object member ("sessionpassword":"...", "password":"...", "apiToken": "...", "client_secret":"..."). A JSON body carries no '=', so neither connection-string detector can see it, and a REST or RPC result body is exactly where a session credential travels in full. THE KEY MUST END WITH THE CREDENTIAL WORD: the closing quote sits immediately after it, so a key that merely CONTAINS one is untouched ("passwordExpiryDays", "passwordPolicy", "tokenCount", "lastPasswordChange", and "accesskeyid", the PUBLIC half of an AWS key pair). The key list is WIDER than the connection-string one (token, secret, credential, passphrase are added) because a quoted key immediately before a ':' is a field name rather than a word in a sentence, which is a far stronger signal than the same word in free prose; widening the '=' list to match would drag those words into prose. Only the value BETWEEN the quotes is replaced, so the object stays parseable JSON. JSON escapes are honoured, so a '\\"' inside a value cannot end the match early and leave a tail of the credential behind. An UNQUOTED value (a JSON number, true/false/null) is NOT matched: the engine replaces a matched span with a placeholder and cannot re-quote it, so redacting one would emit invalid JSON. Object and array values are not matched either: finding their end needs balanced counting, which a regex cannot do.

detectors.name: quoted-key-credential
detectors.description: Credential whose KEY IS WRITTEN AS A STRING in front of an `=`: a PowerShell hashtable, a JSON-ish config literal, an HTTP header name. Both `=` detectors here anchor on a key that runs up to the separator, so a quoted key defeats them, the closing quote sitting between the name and the `=` where the key run cannot cross it. Quoting the key is also the only way to write a header name at all, which is where an API key in a script body actually lives. THE KEY MUST END WITH THE CREDENTIAL WORD, immediately before its closing quote, so a key that merely contains one keeps its value. Only the content between the value's quotes is replaced, so the literal stays parseable and a reader can still see WHICH key was redacted. PROVENANCE: OBSERVED collector literal `_quoted_kv` in the SparkLogs source library (`stdlib/6_pack_finalize.vrl`) at 7bb901b.

detectors.name: env-assignment-credential
detectors.description: Credential in an ENVIRONMENT or CONFIG assignment pasted as a file: `api_key=`, `token:`, `secret=`, `client_secret=`, `access_key=`, the access, auth, refresh and session token spellings, and the hyphen and underscore variants of each. This is the `.env`, `.ini` and YAML shape, which carries a real credential often enough to be worth a detector and is exactly what someone pastes into a browser to ask for help. THE KEY MUST BEGIN THE LINE, allowing indentation and an `export` or `set` prefix, OR FOLLOW A SYSLOG PROCESS TAG (`app[1]: `, `sshd[1234]: `), which is the same assignment forwarded through a log line rather than read from a file. The tag alternative is deliberately narrow: a word character immediately before the bracket, digits inside it, `]:` and exactly one space. A generic `word: ` prefix is NOT admitted, because that is the prose surface that killed the detector this replaces. Requiring the word character excludes `Retry [3]: ` and `step [2]: `; requiring digits excludes `[ERROR]: ` and `[2026-08-25 10:00:00]: `. Together the two alternatives are doing all of the safety work. `token`, `secret` and `key` are ordinary English words: the detector this replaces anchored on them anywhere they appeared, and it redacted `publicKeyToken=`, it redacted the middle of the sentence "The token=X was rejected by the API", and its whitespace-tolerant separator ran across a LINE BREAK into the next line's first token. A key that starts its own line is a field name; the same word inside a sentence is a word. THREE MORE NARROWING RULES, each closing one of those failures. The key ENDS at the separator, so `secret_name:`, `token_count:` and `clientSecretExpiry:` keep their values. The separator may carry a run of spaces or tabs on either side, which is the `.ini` `token = value` spelling and the aligned config column; a run of spaces and tabs is safe because it cannot reach off the line, and the detector this replaces crossed a line break because its separator was `\s*`, where `\s` contains `\n`. That is a different character class, not a different quantity of whitespace. And the value is at least EIGHT characters, because a shorter value on one of these keys is a boolean, a placeholder or a word (`true`, `null`, `~`, `see docs`) rather than a credential worth the risk. AN UNQUOTED VALUE STOPS AT A SEMICOLON, which defers to the connection-string grammar: several of these keys also name a connection-string field, and without the rule this detector would swallow the `;` terminator and the neighbouring keys that the connection-string detector exists to preserve. There is deliberately NO unterminated-quote branch here either: eating to the end of a line is the right trade for a tool-anchored pattern and the wrong one for a key list this broad. KNOWN AND ACCEPTED: an unsigiled assignment MID-LINE with no syslog tag in front of it is not matched at all, which is the deliberate price of retiring the bare-word detector and is pinned in the corpus so the trade stays visible. A footnote-shaped `note[1]: ` prefix does satisfy the tag rule. And a sentence that BEGINS with one of these words and a colon loses its first word if that word is eight characters or longer (`secret: successfully rotated` becomes `secret: <fake> rotated`). One word of prose is the price of the config shape, and the cases are pinned in the tests so the behaviour is a decision on the record.

detectors.name: msi-property-credential
detectors.description: Credential passed as an installer PUBLIC PROPERTY on a setup command line (`msiexec /i agent.msi /qn TOKEN=...`, `setup.exe /S /v"/qn AUTHKEY=..."`). This is how an RMM, backup or monitoring agent receives its tenant secret at install time, which makes it the one credential a managed fleet definitionally puts on a command line. THE DETECTOR IS CASE-SENSITIVE AND THAT IS ITS ENTIRE SAFETY CLAIM: only a property spelt in full uppercase can be set from a command line, so requiring uppercase is what keeps this off the camelCase and PascalCase assembly-identity fields that carry the same words. It must never be given the `i` flag. The name ENDS with the credential word, so `TOKENFILE=` and `SECRETSTORE=` keep their values, and the site, tenant, customer id, log path and installer path all survive. The escaped-quote branch comes first because a property inside a `/v"..."` wrapper arrives with its own quotes backslash-escaped.

detectors.name: putty-password-flag
detectors.description: Password given to the PuTTY family (`plink`, `pscp`, `psftp`, `putty`) with `-pw`. The anchor is the tool name plus the flag plus an IMMEDIATE separator, and the separator is the safety claim: it is what excludes `-pwfile`, which names a path that must survive because the path is diagnostic and the secret is not on that line. The tool name is what keeps a bare `-pw` on any other command line out of scope, and the gap between the tool and the flag stops at a command separator so the match cannot reach into the next command.

detectors.name: sql-cli-password-flag
detectors.description: Password given to a SQL Server command-line tool (`sqlcmd`, `osql`, `bcp`, `isql`) with the uppercase `-P` flag. THE CASE OF THAT ONE LETTER IS THE WHOLE DISTINCTION: lowercase `-p` on these tools prints performance statistics and carries no secret. The detector is therefore case-SENSITIVE, and the tool names are spelt as character classes rather than matched with the `i` flag, because JavaScript has no inline case-sensitivity group and the tool name genuinely is case-insensitive while the flag genuinely is not.

detectors.name: psexec-password-flag
detectors.description: Password given to Sysinternals PsExec (`psexec`, `psexec64`) with `-p`, attached or spaced. THE HYPHEN IS PART OF THE ANCHOR: `/p` is left alone, so a path token ending in `psexec` followed by another program's `/P` cannot have its neighbour taken. The flag is matched case-SENSITIVELY and the tool name is spelt as character classes rather than matched with the `i` flag, because JavaScript has no inline case-sensitivity group and the tool name genuinely is case-insensitive while the flag is not. The gap between the tool and the flag stops at a command separator so the match cannot reach into the next command.

detectors.name: schtasks-runas-password
detectors.description: Run-as password given to Task Scheduler with `/RP value` or `/RP:value`. THE TOOL BASENAME IS THE SAFETY CLAIM: `/RP` is two letters and would be a free gift as a global word, so it is only read as a password flag on a `schtasks` command line. A separator after `/RP` is required, which is what stops a longer flag from being claimed as an attached value, and the gap between the tool and the flag stops at a command separator so the match cannot reach into the next command.

detectors.name: mysql-password-flag
detectors.description: Password given to `mysql` or `mysqldump` ATTACHED to `-p` (`-phunter2`). ONLY THE ATTACHED FORM CARRIES A SECRET: a spaced next token is the database name, because `mysql -p mydatabase` prompts for the password rather than putting it on the line, so no separator is allowed after the flag and `-p mydatabase` survives. Uppercase `-P` is the port and there is no `/p` spelling, so the flag is matched case-SENSITIVELY and the tool name is spelt as character classes, JavaScript having no inline case-sensitivity group.

detectors.name: command-flag-password
detectors.description: Credential given to any tool as a SIGIL-PREFIXED word flag: `-password:`, `/pwd:`, `--pass=`, `-passphrase=`, `-token=`, `/session-token:`. THE SIGIL AND THE IMMEDIATE SEPARATOR ARE THE ANCHOR, and together they are what makes a word list this broad safe. `token` inside a longer identifier is unreachable, since `publicKeyToken=` has no sigil in front of it and `-tokenfile=` has more word characters between the word and the separator. Anchoring on a flag LETTER instead was measured against real command lines and abandoned: a single letter names something different on every tool. The `password=` and `pwd=` spellings without a sigil are the key=value detector's job, so the bare-word forms here take a colon only, and the value may not start with `<` or `*` because those are a redirection and a prompt placeholder rather than a credential.

detectors.name: powershell-securestring-argument
detectors.description: Plaintext argument handed straight to `ConvertTo-SecureString` positionally, either before or after its `-AsPlainText` and `-Force` switches. The cmdlet name is a proper noun with one meaning, and the value that follows it positionally is by definition the plaintext being wrapped. `-AsPlainText` MUST APPEAR SOMEWHERE ON THE COMMAND, because the cmdlet itself rejects a plaintext argument without it: `ConvertTo-SecureString $s` reads an already encrypted string, and the cmdlet named in a sentence is a sentence. ONE SHAPE IS EXEMPT FROM THAT REQUIREMENT: a quoted value whose quote never closes before the end of the line, which is how script-block logging splits one command across two events. A quote opened and abandoned cannot be prose, so the shape alone carries the redaction. IT STANDS DOWN WHEN THE NAMED SPELLING APPEARS LATER ON THE LINE, which is what the look-ahead is for: in `ConvertTo-SecureString ... -String <value>` the value belongs to the named parameter and is matched by the sibling detector instead. Without that, a zero-width anchor would claim the word immediately after the cmdlet name AND the named value, because unlike a replacement template a look-behind cannot absorb the text between them. The value may not begin with `$`, `-`, `(`, `@`, `[`, `<`, `*` or `/`: those open a variable, another parameter, an expression, a splat, a redirection or a path, none of which is a plaintext credential. PROVENANCE: OBSERVED collector literal `_ctss_arg` in the SparkLogs source library (`stdlib/6_pack_finalize.vrl`) at 7bb901b.

detectors.name: powershell-securestring-string-argument
detectors.description: The same credential given to `ConvertTo-SecureString` through its named `-String` parameter. It is a separate detector rather than an optional hop in the sibling, because an optional hop in front of a zero-width anchor matches BOTH with and without it and would redact twice.

detectors.name: powershell-securestring-pipe
detectors.description: A quoted literal piped into `ConvertTo-SecureString`. Here the credential comes FIRST and the cmdlet name after it, so the cmdlet is the look-ahead and the quoted literal is the match. Only a literal is matched: a piped variable or command output is not a credential in the text.

detectors.name: powershell-secret-parameter
detectors.description: Quoted literal given to a PowerShell named secret parameter (`-Password`, `-PlainTextPassword`, `-ApiKey`, `-ClientSecret`, `-SasToken`, `-AccessToken`, `-Token`, `-Secret` and the hyphen and underscore spellings). THE MATCH IS THE CONTENT BETWEEN THE QUOTES, not the quoted run, so the quoting around the value survives and the command still reads as a command. A quoted value is required: an unquoted argument after one of these parameters is as often a variable or a splat as a literal, and the quotes are what make the literal a literal. A value whose quote never closes is redacted to the end of the line rather than left half-matched.

detectors.name: powershell-secret-parameter-single-quoted
detectors.description: The single-quoted form of the same parameter list, as its own detector because the run of content has to know which quote character closes it.

detectors.name: powershell-secret-parameter-unquoted
detectors.description: UNQUOTED value after a COMPOUND PowerShell secret parameter (`-AccountPassword`, `-NewPassword`, `-ApiKey`, `-ClientSecret`, `-SharedAccessKey`, `-SasToken`, `-AccessToken`, `-SessionToken`, and the hyphen and underscore spellings). THE SPLIT FROM THE QUOTED PARAMETER DETECTORS IS A PROSE DECISION RATHER THAN A SYNTAX ONE. `-Password`, `-Token` and `-Secret` are words an operator writes in a sentence, and a space-terminated value branch on those turns 'the -Password parameter is optional' into a redaction of the word `parameter`; those keep the quoted-only rule, which costs little because PowerShell already requires quoting for any value holding a space. The keys here are compound identifiers, rarer in prose but not absent from it, and that is the trade this row makes rather than avoids: a sentence naming `-ApiKey` loses the word after it. One word of a log line, in exchange for the one-liner assembled from variables that prints its secret without quotes. `[a-z]+password` REQUIRES A PREFIX, which leaves the bare `-Password` spelling to the quoted rule.
